newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia's central government structure agreed.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia's central government structure agreed.

text.p: After two and a half months of wrangling, Bosnia's three-member Presidency has finally agreed a structure for its weak central government, the German diplomat who brokered the deal announced on Saturday.

The country's tripartite Presidency will preside over a Council of Ministers whose convolutions are intended to ensure that none of Bosnia's three ethnic communities -- Moslem, Croat and Serb -- is disadvantaged.

"I am very happy to say the three Presidency members reached an agreement," Ambassador Michael Steiner, deputy to the international community's High Representative in Bosnia, told reporters in Sarajevo.
"I know that just by having this new Council of Ministers we will not enter paradise...But then we have to ask ourselves what is the choice? It is the only way we have to go."

Steiner said the Council of Ministers will be headed by two co-chairmen who will function essentially as co-Prime Ministers. One will be a Serb and the other a Moslem, and they will have a Vice-Chairman who is a Croat.

Under them will be three ministers -- a Minister for Foreign Affairs (a Croat), a Minister for Civil Affairs and Communications (a Serb) and a Minister for Foreign Trade and Economic Relations (a Moslem).
Each minister will have two deputies, one from each ethnic community other than his or her own.
The Council of Ministers is supposed to meet at least weekly and the co-Chairmen will alternate at meetings.
"It is a structure which takes into account that after the war there is much mistrust," Steiner said of the unwieldy system.
The ambassador indicated he would have preferred five ministers and described the agreed arrangement as "a bit too compact".
The broad outline of Bosnia's post-war government was laid down in the Dayton peace agreement of December 1995.

Dayton called for a single sovereign state within Bosnia's pre-war borders consisting of a Moslem-Croat Federation and a Serb Republic. Most government responsibilities were assigned to the two entities, making for a weak central government.
National elections in September decided who would fill the tripartite Presidency, but those three men had not been able to agree until Saturday on a Council of Ministers.

Steiner said the next step in the process would be for specific names to be offered up for each Council of Ministers positions for Parliamentary consideration. He said he hoped the body would be seated within a week.
Formation of the Council of Ministers is likely to be hailed as evidence of significant progress in Bosnia at two major international gatherings next week.
A summit meeting is to be held in Lisbon followed by a Dayton implementation conference in London. The goal of both meetings is to set priorities for the peace process as it enters its second year.
